conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I’ve had this bad pain in my upper belly for a few days. It’s right here—across the top, near the middle. Hurts worse when I cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been throwing up—mostly the alcohol I was drinking. Haven’t eaten in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how much have you been drinking lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I relapsed. For about two weeks, I’ve been drinking over a liter of brandy and tequila every day. I thought I could just have one… but it got out of control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. When was your last drink?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Around 4 a.m. yesterday. I stopped because I felt so bad—shaky, sweating, like ants crawling under my skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like alcohol withdrawal. We’ll monitor that closely. You’ve been through this before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… more than once. I’ve been sober for months before, but this time… I just felt helpless. My daughter’s making bad choices, and I don’t know how to help her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really tough. We can talk more about support later. For now, we’re treating your withdrawal with diazepam—it helps with the tremors and anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I haven’t taken my Suboxone either. I stop it when I drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding your Suboxone for now because of the Valium. Once your withdrawal is under control, we’ll restart it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. My stomach pain—is it from the drinking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, yes. We did a CT scan and ultrasound. Your liver shows signs of cirrhosis and portal hypertension—scarring and increased pressure. That can stretch the liver capsule and cause pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cirrhosis? I knew my liver wasn’t great, but… is it bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s damage, but it’s not end-stage. The good news is your liver enzymes, while elevated, aren’t extremely high. We’re treating this as mild alcoholic hepatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So… no steroids or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Steroids are for more severe cases. We’re focusing on stopping alcohol, giving you IV fluids, vitamins, and medications to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been skipping my omeprazole and vitamins… I know I shouldn’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted those. You’re getting thiamine, folate, multivitamins—important to prevent complications. And we’ve added ranitidine for stomach comfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show improvement. Your acidosis—high anion gap—is resolving. That was from the alcohol binge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your bicarbonate is up, anion gap is down. That’s a good sign your body is recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver numbers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: AST and ALT are still elevated but trending down. Bilirubin is improving too. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel shaky. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re using the CIWA scale to track your withdrawal symptoms. Your score is low now, so we’re tapering the Valium slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared of having seizures or DTs. I’ve heard about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re preventing that with the medication. You haven’t had seizures before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I don’t think so. But I’ve been admitted five times for withdrawal. Once in ICU.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you safe. You’re doing well so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal pain is better today, I hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s much less. Still bloated, but not tender anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. The CT showed no pancreatitis, which we were worried about. The pain was likely from liver and spleen swelling, plus vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the varices? The report mentioned large ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, portal hypertension can cause varices—enlarged veins in the esophagus. That’s why you’re on nadolol. It lowers the pressure to reduce bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been skipping that too… I’ll try to be better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you stay on track. You have a follow-up with hepatology next week. They may do an endoscopy to check the varices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lab results this morning look good. Your liver tests are continuing to improve. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. Will I get my Suboxone before I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll give you one dose today and send you home with a prescription. It’s important to restart it and stay on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want my PCP to know about this relapse yet. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll coordinate care, but your treatment is confidential. We’ll focus on supporting your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ashamed… I was doing so well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Relapse is part of recovery for many people. What matters is that you’re here, getting help, and want to stop. That takes courage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. We’ve reviewed your discharge meds. All your previous ones are continued—omeprazole, Suboxone, nadolol, vitamins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I have the hepatology appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, next week. They’ll discuss long-term liver care. And please keep using your asthma inhalers—your lungs sounded wheezy, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I really want to stay sober this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe in you. Call your support system, go to your meetings, and reach out if you need help. Take care.
